paragraphs.source_en: The ethnographic record shows the most common functions of sites and shelters amongst living African populations. Since these functions are very similar all over the continent, it is possible that they are rooted in a common cultural tradition which originated in prehistoric times or which represents a universal human need. There is therefore no reason to doubt that at least some of these functions existed in the Round Head shelters. Can information from the excavations indicate what the shelters were used for? They partially can. However, the main problem is that the painted shelters have rarely been excavated. No systematic excavation has been done on the Tassili Plateau which is the key area for understanding the possible functions of these important Round Head sites.

paragraphs.source_en: In the Tadrart Acacus, from the nine shelters excavated, only two, Uan Afuda and Uan Muhuggiag, contain Round Head paintings. Although they are in the same wadi and the same altitude, both shelters suggest a different use.

paragraphs.source_en: Uan Muhuggiag has been interpreted as a burial place by Mori (2000) who unearthed the burials of two individuals dated between 7,800 and 5,400 BP. The oldest skeleton was found without any preserved associated artefacts, whereas the more recent individual was found wrapped in a leather sack which was still preserved. This led Mori to suggest a relationship between this evidence and the Round Head painting in the shelter which represented a possible burial scene: anthropomorphic figures standing next to two oval forms were interpreted as living individuals near to dead bodies wrapped in sacks, which is paralleled in the archaeological record (Mori 2000: 178). There is however a difference between the position of the bodies: whereas those excavated were found flexed, those in paintings, supposing they are dead bodies, are represented in a prone position.

paragraphs.source_en: Although Uan Muhuggiag contains burials, its function is unlikely to have been exclusively for funeral purposes. The lithic industry, wild fauna remains and later remains of domesticated cattle and Pastoral pottery indicate that the shelter was occupied or frequented over several millennia, which is not reflected in the number of burials. The function of the shelter was probably multiple and it could also have changed in time.
